name: Capromorelin

lead: Capromorelin is a Pfizer-developed drug that mimics ghrelin. It is sold for pets as Entyce (dogs) and Elura (cats with kidney disease).
In people, a trial in older adults reported a small lean-mass gain, but development in humans was discontinued. No study has tested it for appearance.

paras: It activates the ghrelin/GH secretagogue receptor, raising appetite and growth hormone and IGF-1 levels.
It is a veterinary prescription drug, with vomiting and diarrhoea noted in animals. Human safety data are limited to early-phase and older-adult trials.

lead: Capromorelin is an orally active ghrelin-receptor agonist and growth hormone secretagogue developed by Pfizer. It is approved for veterinary use, as Entyce for appetite stimulation in dogs (US, 2016) and Elura for weight loss in cats with chronic kidney disease (US, 2020).[1][2][2]

Before its veterinary approvals it was studied in humans. A trial in older adults with mild functional limitation tested its effects on hormones, body composition and physical performance.[3] Wikipedia reports that human development was discontinued, as results were not judged strong enough to continue.[1]
No studies have examined capromorelin for cosmetic purposes in healthy people.
infobox: Veterinary prescription drug; not approved for humans[1]

paras: In dogs, capromorelin is indicated for appetite stimulation (US approval May 2016), and in cats for weight loss associated with chronic kidney disease (US approval October 2020).[1][2] Wikipedia notes that the European Medicines Agency approved the feline product as Eluracat.[1] A veterinary review describes it as a novel therapy for stimulating appetite in dogs.[4]

Capromorelin binds the growth hormone secretagogue receptor 1a with high affinity (Ki 7 nM in the original discovery work) and stimulated growth hormone release in rat pituitary cells.[5] It increases growth hormone and IGF-1 levels.[1] In mice, a comparison with ghrelin and GHRP-6 examined its effects on gastric emptying.[6]

Capromorelin is orally absorbed. Medicinal chemistry papers report analogues designed for longer half-lives, and a single-ascending-dose phase 1 trial in people with spinal cord injury and able-bodied volunteers examined its pharmacokinetics.[7][8]
Capromorelin is a pyrazolinone-piperidine dipeptide mimetic, with molecular formula C28H35N5O4 and a molar mass of about 505.6 g/mol.[1][5]

In animals, reported side effects on the veterinary product include vomiting and diarrhoea (Grokipedia, AI-generated).[2] Human safety data come from the early-phase and older-adult studies described below.[3][8]

In a randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled multicentre study in older adults with mild functional limitation, the oral secretagogue was examined for hormonal, body composition and performance effects.[3] Wikipedia summarises the year-long trial of 395 adults aged 65-84 as showing about 1.4 kg of lean mass gain at six months and some improvements in balance and walking, with a planned second year not pursued.[1]

A phase 1 study assessed pharmacokinetics in spinal cord-injured and able-bodied volunteers, and rodent work examined its effect on defecation after spinal cord injury.[8][9] A systematic review of drugs for frailty includes growth hormone secretagogue trials.[10]
Pfizer researchers published the discovery of capromorelin in 2002-2003.[5][5] It was later developed for companion animals.[1][4]
